title: HTTP Authentication: Basic and Digest Access Authentication
summary: Specifies HTTP's authentication framework and two schemes, Basic, which sends a username and password, and Digest, which uses cryptographic hashes so the password is not sent in the clear. It was replaced by RFC 7235, RFC 7615, RFC 7616 and RFC 7617.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives HTTP its authentication framework and two ways to use it. The server sends a challenge, the client answers with proof that it knows the password, and the server checks the answer. Basic puts the password in the request in an easily reversed encoding. Digest never sends the password at all: it sends a hash that mixes the password with a value the server just made up, so a recorded answer cannot be reused for a different request.

subtitle: How HTTP checks that a client knows a password, without sending the password.

tldr.problem: HTTP needs a way for a server to ask a client for proof of identity. The original scheme sent the password across the network in the clear, which anyone listening could read.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a general challenge-and-response framework and two schemes for it. Basic sends a base64-encoded user name and password; Digest sends a hash computed from the password, the server's nonce, the request method and the request URI.
tldr.outcome: An eavesdropper who records a Digest exchange gets one transaction rather than a reusable password. The document was a Draft Standard and has been replaced by RFC 7235, with the two schemes restated in RFC 7616 and RFC 7617.

facts.label: Basic credential encoding
facts.value: Base64 of the userid and password separated by a colon

today: RFC 2617 was published in June 1999 as a Draft Standard. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 7235, RFC 7615, RFC 7616 and RFC 7617. It had itself obsoleted RFC 2069.

sections.title: The Authentication Framework
sections.content:
HTTP provides a simple challenge-response mechanism that a server may use to challenge a client request and a client may use to supply authentication information. It uses an extensible, case-insensitive token to identify the authentication scheme, followed by a comma-separated list of attribute-value pairs carrying the parameters that scheme needs. The grammar is auth-scheme = token and auth-param = token "=" ( token | quoted-string ).

A 401 (Unauthorized) response from an origin server must include a WWW-Authenticate header field carrying at least one challenge for the requested resource. A 407 (Proxy Authentication Required) response from a proxy must include a Proxy-Authenticate header field in the same way. The client answers by sending an Authorization header field, or a Proxy-Authorization header field when it is authenticating to a proxy. The user agent must choose the challenge using the strongest authentication scheme it understands.

Every scheme that issues a challenge must carry a realm directive. The realm value, together with the canonical root URL of the server, defines the protection space: the set of resources on the server that share an authentication scheme and an authorization database. The realm is a string assigned by the server, usually shown to the user so they know which user name and password to use, and there may be several challenges with the same scheme but different realms. The protection space decides where credentials may be reused: if a request has been authorized, the same credentials may be reused for other requests in that space for a period set by the scheme and the user, and unless the scheme says otherwise a protection space cannot extend outside the scope of its server.

If the server does not accept the credentials, it should answer 401 with a new challenge; a proxy does the same with 407. Proxies must be transparent about origin-server authentication: they forward the WWW-Authenticate and Authorization headers untouched.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP authentication is a question and an answer. The server asks with a 401 response that names a scheme, and the client answers with an Authorization header. The scheme also names a realm, which is the area of the site the question covers, so the right user name and password are used for the right part of the site.

sections.title: The Basic Scheme
sections.content:
The Basic scheme is based on the model that the client must authenticate itself with a user-ID and a password for each realm. The realm value should be considered an opaque string that can only be compared for equality with other realms on that server, and the server services the request only if it can validate the user-ID and password for the protection space of the request URI. There are no optional authentication parameters.

The challenge is Basic realm and the credentials are Basic basic-credentials, where the basic credentials are the base64 encoding of the user name and password separated by a single colon. If the user agent wishes to send the userid "Aladdin" and the password "open sesame", the header field is Authorization: Basic QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==. The base64 encoding is not limited to 76 characters per line.

A client may assume that all paths at or deeper than the depth of the last symbolic element in the path of the request URI are inside the protection space named by the current challenge, and it may send the Authorization header preemptively for resources in that space without waiting for another challenge.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic is the simplest scheme there is. The server names a realm, the client sends the user name and password joined by a colon, and the whole thing is base64 encoded, which hides it from casual reading but not from anyone who decodes it. The RFC is clear that this sends the password in an unencrypted form.

sections.title: The Digest Scheme
sections.content:
Digest is also a challenge-response paradigm, but it challenges using a nonce value. A valid response contains a checksum, by default the MD5 checksum, of the user name, the password, the given nonce value, the HTTP method and the requested URI. In this way the password is never sent in the clear. As with Basic, the user name and password must be prearranged by some means this document does not address.

An optional header lets the server name the algorithm used to create the checksum. By default MD5 is used, and it is the only algorithm described in this document. An MD5 digest of 128 bits is represented as 32 printable ASCII characters: the bits are taken from most significant to least significant, four at a time, and each group of four is written in hexadecimal.

The RFC is careful about what Digest is not. It provides no encryption of the message content, and it is not intended as a complete answer to the need for security on the World Wide Web; the intent is simply to create an access authentication method that avoids the most serious flaws of Basic. It is a password-based system and on the server side suffers from all the same problems as any password system, and it makes no provision for the initial secure arrangement between user and server that establishes the password. Users and implementors are told to be aware that it is not as secure as Kerberos, nor as secure as any client-side private-key scheme, though it is better than nothing, better than what is commonly used with telnet and ftp, and better than Basic authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Digest replaces the password with a fingerprint. The fingerprint is computed from the password together with a random-looking value the server just sent, the request method and the address being fetched, so it is different for every request and cannot be turned back into the password. What it does not do is hide the content of the request or the response.

sections.title: The Headers That Carry a Digest
sections.content:
When a server receives a request for a protected object and no acceptable Authorization header, it answers with a 401 status and a WWW-Authenticate header. For Digest the header is challenge = "Digest" digest-challenge, where the challenge may carry realm, domain, nonce, opaque, stale, algorithm and qop-options.

The realm is a string displayed to users so they know which user name and password to use, and it should contain at least the name of the host performing the authentication. The domain is a quoted, space-separated list of URIs defining the protection space; any URI that has one of these as a prefix, after both are made absolute, may be assumed to be in the same protection space, and if the directive is omitted or empty the client should assume the protection space is all URIs on the responding server. The nonce is a server-specified string that should be uniquely generated each time a 401 response is made, and it is opaque to the client; the RFC suggests it might be built from a time-stamp, the ETag of the requested entity and a private key known only to the server, which lets the server limit how long the nonce stays valid and prevents a replayed request for an updated version of the resource. The opaque string is returned unchanged by the client in later requests. The stale flag says the previous request was rejected because the nonce was stale: if it is TRUE the client may retry with a new response without asking the user for new credentials, and if it is anything else the user name or password is wrong and new values are needed. The algorithm directive names the pair of algorithms used, MD5 being the default, and an unrecognised algorithm means the challenge should be ignored. The qop directive lists the quality of protection values the server supports, auth for authentication and auth-int for authentication with integrity protection.

The client retries the request with an Authorization header whose directives are username, realm, nonce, digest-uri, response, and optionally algorithm, cnonce, opaque, qop and nonce-count. The digest-uri repeats the request URI because a proxy is allowed to change the request line in transit. The cnonce is a client-chosen value that must be present when a qop directive was sent and must be absent when one was not; it is used to avoid chosen plaintext attacks, to provide mutual authentication and to give some message integrity protection. The nonce-count is the hexadecimal count of requests sent with that nonce, and the server detects a replay by noticing the same count twice. If a directive or its value is improper, or a required directive is missing, the right response is 400 Bad Request; if the request digest is invalid, the failure should be logged, because repeated failures from one client may mean someone is guessing passwords.

A third header, Authentication-Info, lets the server pass information back about a successful authentication. Its nextnonce directive names the nonce the client should use next, which is how one-time or changing nonces are implemented; if the client ignores it, the next request may come back with stale set to TRUE. The optional response-auth directive holds a response digest that supports mutual authentication, the server proving that it knows the user's secret, and with qop=auth-int it also gives limited integrity protection of the response.
sections.plainLanguage: The server's challenge and the client's answer are both lists of labelled values. The server sends a realm, a nonce and a list of the kinds of protection it will accept. The client sends back its name, the nonce it was given, the address it wants, a counter, and the fingerprint. The server can then check the fingerprint, and can send back a next nonce so the client uses a fresh one next time.

sections.title: How the Response Is Computed
sections.content:
The RFC uses two shorthands: KD(secret, data) for the digest algorithm applied to a secret and some data, and H(data) for the checksum algorithm applied to data. For MD5 and MD5-sess, H(data) = MD5(data) and KD(secret, data) = H(concat(secret, ":", data)), so the digest is the MD5 of the secret, a colon and the data.

Two strings feed the calculation. A1 is the user name, a colon, the realm and a colon and the password: A1 = unq(username-value) ":" unq(realm-value) ":" passwd. With the MD5-sess algorithm A1 is computed only once, on the first request after a challenge, as H(username ":" realm ":" passwd) ":" nonce ":" cnonce, which creates a session key that differs for each authentication session and limits the amount of material hashed with any one key. A2 is the request method, a colon and the request URI: A2 = Method ":" digest-uri-value, and with qop=auth-int the hash of the entity body is appended, giving A2 = Method ":" digest-uri-value ":" H(entity-body).

The response value itself is 32 hex digits. With qop set to auth or auth-int it is KD(H(A1), nonce ":" nc ":" cnonce ":" qop ":" H(A2)). Without a qop directive, for compatibility with the earlier RFC 2069, it is KD(H(A1), nonce ":" H(A2)). The server checks the header by looking up the password for the submitted user name, performing the same digest operation, and comparing the result with the value sent. The server does not actually need the cleartext password: as long as it has H(A1), the validity of the header can be verified.

The quoted-string notation needs care. The values of many directives are quoted strings, but the surrounding quotation marks are removed when the string A1 is formed, and no white space is allowed in the strings passed to the hash function unless that white space was inside the quoted string or entity body being digested. The example in the RFC shows that with username="Mufasa" and realm=myhost@testrealm.com and the password "Circle Of Life", the digested string is Mufasa:myhost@testrealm.com:Circle Of Life with no quotation marks and no white space around the colons.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint is built in two halves. The first half mixes in the password, the user name and the realm. The second half mixes in the request itself, such as the method and the address, and the server's nonce. The two halves are hashed together. Because the nonce changes every time, the same password produces a different answer each time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Basic authentication is not a secure method of user authentication and does nothing to protect the entity, which crosses the network in cleartext. Because it transmits passwords in the clear it should not be used, without enhancements, to protect sensitive or valuable information. It is commonly used for identification rather than access control, and that is only safe if the server issues both the user name and the password and does not let the user choose it, because naive users reuse one password to avoid keeping several. If users pick their own passwords, the danger is not only access to the documents but access to anything else the user protects with the same password, and a password database that is not kept secure exposes users of that system to unauthorized access elsewhere. Basic is also vulnerable to spoofing by counterfeit servers, which can request a password, store it and fake an error; Digest does not have this problem.

Digest does not provide a strong authentication mechanism when compared with public key mechanisms. The greatest threat to the transactions these protocols serve is network snooping. With Basic, an eavesdropper obtains the user's password, which gives access to the database and to everything else protected by that password. With Digest, the eavesdropper gets access to the transaction in question and not to the password; the information gained permits a replay attack, but only for the same document, and even that may be limited by the server's choice of nonce.

Replay attacks need care. A replay of a simple GET request is usually pointless, since the URI is hashed into the request and the server only delivers that document, but under Basic the stolen password opens every document. For transactions where no replay can be tolerated, the server can use one-time nonce values, at the cost of remembering which nonces have been used until the nonce's time-stamp expires. POST and PUT requests need special attention: unless the server uses one-time or limited-use nonces, or insists on qop=auth-int, an attacker can replay valid credentials with counterfeit form data. Even with integrity protection, most metadata in header fields is not protected.

The RFC closes with a summary: by modern cryptographic standards Digest is weak, but it is valuable as a replacement for Basic, it remedies some but not all of Basic's weaknesses, and its strength varies with the implementation, in particular with the structure of the nonce. Any compliant implementation will be relatively weak by cryptographic standards, but any compliant implementation will be far superior to Basic authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic is not safe on its own, because the password crosses the network where anyone can read it, and people tend to use one password everywhere, so leaking it leaks more than one site. Digest is much better: what a listener records is a value tied to one request. It is still not strong, and the server has to think about nonce design and replay, which the RFC covers at length.

viz.caption: THE DIGEST EXCHANGE FROM THE EXAMPLE IN SECTION 3.5

messages.label: GET /dir/index.html
messages.note: No Authorization header is sent, because the client has not authenticated yet.

messages.label: 401 Unauthorized
messages.note: WWW-Authenticate carries the realm, the quality of protection values, a nonce and an opaque value.

messages.label: GET with Authorization: Digest
messages.note: The client returns the user name, the nonce, the URI, a counter, its own nonce and the response digest.

messages.label: 200 OK
messages.note: The server compares its own digest with the one sent and may return Authentication-Info.

viz.caption: THE DIGEST CALCULATION, RESTATED FROM SECTION 3.2.2

data.title: Computing the response value
data.code:
A1 = username ":" realm ":" password
A2 = method ":" uri          (plus H(entity-body) when qop=auth-int)

response = KD( H(A1), nonce ":" nc ":" cnonce ":" qop ":" H(A2) )

where KD(secret, data) = H(secret ":" data)
and H(data) = MD5(data) by default

cells: The user name and password, base64 encoded
A digest computed from the password and the request
One transaction, which may allow a replay
